links.note: Asks what globalisation is; the answer gives the integration of national economies through trade, investment, capital flows and technology - 23810's definition. 23811 is the sibling listing what moves; this stem asks for the process itself.
Why India put barriers on trade and investment (protecting infant industries in the 1950s-60s) and why it removed them in the 1990s - 23814, tariffs and quotas and their removal as liberalisation.

Flexibility in labour laws letting companies employ workers only when needed is 23818 - competition making employment flexible and insecure. 23817 is the pressure on producers; this item is about what that pressure does to labour.

The ways MNCs set up or control production abroad: buying out domestic companies, making them produce for them, placing orders with small producers. That is 23807, MNCs producing jointly with or through local companies. 23806 is the money put in; 23805 is where they choose to go.
The answer argues entirely from the WTO - started at the developed countries' initiative, its rules forcing developing countries to drop barriers while developed countries kept theirs. 23815.

'The impact has not been uniform' with the answer naming small producers of batteries, plastics, toys and dairy hit by cheaper imports, and flexibly employed workers - the uneven distribution of gains that 23819 addresses. 23817 and 23818 are the two mechanisms this answer cites.
How liberalisation of trade and investment policy helped globalisation - goods importable and exportable freely, companies free to set up abroad. 23814.

How foreign trade integrates markets across countries, with a worked example - 23809 exactly (markets connected so choices and prices in one affect the other). 23808 states that trade creates the opportunity; this item asks about the integration it produces.

Speculative essay on globalisation continuing; the answer opens by restating globalisation as integration through foreign trade and investment and names its drivers, which is 23810. Its second half moves toward 23819.

Two opposed arguments to be weighed - small producers annihilated and jobs insecure against better product quality. Weighing who gains and who loses is 23819. Same concept as qid:87484, which asks the same thing as a statement.

Six-blank chain whose first and governing blank is 'globalisation', with foreign trade, investment and competition following. 23810. 23816 would fit if the item stopped at buyers' greater choice, but the blanks run through the whole process.

Three-part MCQ; part (1) keys 'goods, services and investments' and excludes people, which is precisely 23811's point that movement of people has lagged behind goods, services and investment. Parts (2) and (3) reach 23807 and 23819.
The WTO as the body pressing liberalisation of foreign trade and investment - 23815, against IMF, ILO and WHO.
Investment as money spent to buy assets such as land is 23806's description verbatim; the distractors are consumption spending.

SEZs set up to attract foreign investment are the favourable government policy in 23805 (MNCs locate where markets, labour and government policy suit them) - world-class facilities and a five-year tax holiday. 23814 covers the removal of trade barriers rather than incentives to locate.

Who is harmed by MNC entry - the mechanism is competition forcing costs down and quality up, which weaker producers cannot meet: 23817. DEFECT: this item and qid:105838 are the same stem with DIFFERENT keys - here 'all substandard domestic producers', there 'all small scale producers'. The chapter says small producers were hit hard, so this row's key is the doubtful one.
Ford Motors' first Indian plant near Chennai is the chapter's worked example of an MNC producing in collaboration with a local company (Mahindra & Mahindra), which is 23807.
MNCs setting up abroad where production costs are low so profits are greater is 23805's description - locating where it is cheap and conditions are favourable.

The most common route for MNC investment - 23807, buying up local companies and expanding production. DEFECT: the key is marked 'set up new factories'. The text says the commonest route is to buy existing local companies, which is option B and is how qid:87490 part (2) keys the same question. This key is wrong.
Same stem as qid:105830, keyed to small-scale producers, which matches the chapter. Concept is 23817, competition from MNCs and cheaper imports bearing on the weakest producers.

Which sector benefited least is a question about the uneven spread of globalisation's gains, 23819. DEFECT: the option set is broken - 'Industrial Sector' and 'Secondary Sector' are the same thing, so two of the four options are duplicates.

External rather than internal trade as what contributes to globalisation is 23808 - trade reaching beyond the domestic market. The internal/external contrast is the whole of the item, which is why it sits here rather than on 23810's broader definition.
Investment as spending on factory buildings, machines and equipment - 23806's assets clause. Same concept as qid:105827.

Three of the four options are the chapter's enabling factors (technology, liberalisation of trade, WTO) and the odd one out is bank nationalisation. Of the four candidate concepts (23812, 23813, 23814, 23815) I have taken 23814, the policy factor the chapter treats as the principal driver and the one the WTO option hangs off.

Cheaper imports replacing demand for domestic production and slowing agriculture and industry is the competitive pressure of 23817. 23819 is the response to that pressure rather than the pressure itself.
